cases.question: What do sections 22 and 290 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act say about VAT returns?

claims.text: A taxable person must submit a VAT return to the Service in the prescribed form on or before the 21st day of the following month, with or without a notice, and whether or not an economic activity has taken place.
If the Service grants an extension of the period for filing returns under section 22, this does not extend the time to pay the tax.
The returns must contain the input tax paid, output tax collected and VAT payable on all taxable supplies in the preceding month.
The filing rule in section 22(1) does not apply to a small business.

A small business may, subject to a written notice addressed to the Service, choose to opt out of the exemption granted to small businesses under this Part, including registration, charging of tax on its taxable supplies and filing of returns.
The opt-out choice in section 22(5) does not apply to companies engaged in petroleum operations as defined in the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025.
A business that ceases to be a small business shall file monthly VAT returns.

In deciding whether a person meets the small company threshold, the value of two kinds of taxable supplies is excluded: supply of a capital asset of the person, and supply made solely as a consequence of selling the whole or part of the business or permanently ceasing to carry on business.
A taxable person granted the exemption in subsection (4) is exempt from sections 105 and 107 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act and section 152 of the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025.
Where the Service deploys technology, a taxable person shall render returns in real time or at such other time as the Service may prescribe.
For the purpose of attribution, any VAT return under section 22 shall give details of consumption of taxable supplies, irrespective of where the return is filed.

A non-resident person who derives only passive income from investment in Nigeria may not be required to register for tax, but shall provide relevant information as may be prescribed by the Service.
Every ministry, department or agency of the Federal or a State government, and every Local Government, shall register for tax and obtain a Tax ID.
The relevant tax authority may issue guidelines to give effect to the non-resident registration provision.
"Registration" means the action or process of registering or of being registered for tax purposes in accordance with the Act.

gaps.text: The passages do not say whether the asker is a taxable person, a non-resident person, or a government body, so the asker's own position cannot be determined.

cases.rendered:
Every taxable person shall register with the relevant tax authority and obtain a Taxpayer Identification ("Tax ID") for the purpose of compliance with tax obligations. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 4]

A non-resident person that supplies taxable goods or services to any person in Nigeria, or derives income from Nigeria, shall register for tax purposes and obtain a Tax ID. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 6]

A non-resident person who derives only passive income from investment in Nigeria may not be required to register for tax, but shall provide relevant information as may be prescribed by the Service. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 6]

Every ministry, department or agency of the Federal or a State government, and every Local Government, shall register for tax and obtain a Tax ID. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 5]

The relevant tax authority may issue guidelines to give effect to the non-resident registration provision. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 6]

"Registration" means the action or process of registering or of being registered for tax purposes in accordance with the Act. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "registration"]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The passages do not say whether the asker is a taxable person, a non-resident person, or a government body, so the asker's own position cannot be determined.
- The passages do not define who counts as a taxable person.
- The guidelines the relevant tax authority may issue, and the information the Service may prescribe, are not among the passages.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 4 (gazette page A 266)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 6 (gazette pages A 266, A 267)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 5 (gazette page A 266)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "registration" (gazette page A 331)

cases.question: I filed my company's VAT return three months late. What is the total penalty?

claims.text: A taxable person who fails or refuses to file returns, or knowingly files incomplete or inaccurate returns, to the relevant tax authority in accordance with the Act is liable to an administrative penalty of ₦100,000 in the first month in which the failure occurs.
The same provision adds an administrative penalty of ₦50,000 for each subsequent month in which the failure continues.
Separately, where any tax is not paid within the period prescribed under the Act, a sum equal to 10% of the amount of tax payable is added to it, subject to section 67 of the Act.

Where tax is not paid within the prescribed period, naira remittances carry interest at the prevailing monetary policy rate of the Central Bank of Nigeria plus a spread to be determined by the Minister, from the date the tax becomes payable until it is paid.
The penalty and interest under section 65 are not treated as part of the tax paid for the purpose of claiming relief under the Act or any other tax law.

gaps: The total amount needs a calculation of the monthly penalties, which is not done here.
The passages do not say whether the late-filing penalty counts three months as the first month plus two subsequent months, or how the months are counted.
The passages do not say that the section 101 penalty applies to a VAT return specifically, or what return periods and deadlines apply to VAT returns.
The passages do not say whether the VAT was paid on time, so it is unclear whether the 10% addition and interest apply.
Section 67 of the Act, which section 65 is subject to, is not among the passages.
The spread set by the Minister is not among the passages.

cases.rendered:
A taxable person who fails or refuses to file returns, or knowingly files incomplete or inaccurate returns, to the relevant tax authority in accordance with the Act is liable to an administrative penalty of ₦100,000 in the first month in which the failure occurs. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 101]

The same provision adds an administrative penalty of ₦50,000 for each subsequent month in which the failure continues. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 101]

Separately, where any tax is not paid within the period prescribed under the Act, a sum equal to 10% of the amount of tax payable is added to it, subject to section 67 of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65]

Where tax is not paid within the prescribed period, naira remittances carry interest at the prevailing monetary policy rate of the Central Bank of Nigeria plus a spread to be determined by the Minister, from the date the tax becomes payable until it is paid. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65]

The penalty and interest under section 65 are not treated as part of the tax paid for the purpose of claiming relief under the Act or any other tax law. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The total amount needs a calculation of the monthly penalties, which is not done here.
- The passages do not say whether the late-filing penalty counts three months as the first month plus two subsequent months, or how the months are counted.
- The passages do not say that the section 101 penalty applies to a VAT return specifically, or what return periods and deadlines apply to VAT returns.
- The passages do not say whether the VAT was paid on time, so it is unclear whether the 10% addition and interest apply.
- Section 67 of the Act, which section 65 is subject to, is not among the passages.
- The spread set by the Minister is not among the passages.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 101 (gazette page A 312)

- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65: Only the cited text makes the interest in subsection (1)(b) and (c) compound and applies it to tax debts unpaid at commencement. (DR-245)

<question>

</question>
<gaps>

cases.rendered:
Where, in a year of assessment, a company's effective tax rate is less than 15%, the company shall recompute and pay an additional tax that makes its effective tax rate equal to 15%. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57]

This rule applies to a company that is a constituent entity of an MNE group, and to any other company with an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57]

"Effective tax rate" means the aggregate covered tax paid by the company for the year divided by the company's profits. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57]

For this section, "profits" means the net profits before tax as reported in the audited financial statement less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost for the year. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57]

"Multinational group" means MNE group. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "multinational group"]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The top-up amount needs a calculation using the profits as defined and the covered tax paid, which the law does not give as a figure here and which is not done here.
- The passages do not say whether the company is a constituent entity of an MNE group, or what makes a company a constituent entity or an MNE group member.
- The passages do not say whether the profits figure given matches the definition of profits (net profits before tax in the audited financial statement less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost).
- The passages do not say what counts as covered tax paid.
- Subsection (3) of section 57 is not printed in the passages.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57 (gazette page A 426)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "multinational group" (gazette page A 506)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)

A donation of a revenue or capital nature may be deducted from the profits of that period.

The total deduction allowed to a company under section 164 for any year of assessment shall not exceed an amount equal to 10% of the company's profit before tax for that year.
For a donation other than in cash, the value for section 164 is the lower of the market value at the time of the donation or the consideration paid for the item when it was acquired.

claims.text: VAT is paid on all taxable supplies in Nigeria, subject to the exemptions in Part IV of Chapter Eight of the Act.
VAT is charged on the value of all taxable supplies at the rate of 7.5%, subject to the provisions of Part IV of Chapter Eight of the Act.
The value of an imported taxable supply is the price of the taxable supply imported plus two kinds of amounts.
The first kind is taxes, duties and other charges levied either outside or by reason of importation into Nigeria, other than VAT imposed under the Act.

cases.rationale: ntaa2025:s72 subsections (2) to (4): banks and government bodies demand a certificate for the three years before the current year of assessment for the listed transactions.
cases.question: Why would my bank ask for a tax clearance certificate, and how many years must it cover?

claims.text: Any Ministry, department or agency of Government or any commercial bank with which a person has dealings on the transactions listed in subsection (4) shall demand from that person a tax clearance certificate of three years immediately preceding the current year of assessment.

The listed transactions are: application for a certificate of occupancy; approval of building plans; application for award of contract by government or its agencies; application for a firearms licence; application for an import and export licence; and application for a trade licence.

A tax clearance certificate shall disclose, for the last three years of assessment, total profits or chargeable income, tax payable, tax paid, and tax outstanding or alternatively a statement that no tax is due.

The relevant tax authority shall issue a certificate within two weeks of the person's demand, or give reasons for denial, where it is of the opinion that the tax assessed on the person's profits or income has been fully paid or that no tax is due.

gaps: The passages do not say which specific transaction, if any, the bank is dealing with in the reader's case, so they do not show whether the bank's request falls under the listed transactions.
The passages do not state any other reason a bank may ask for a certificate.

cases.question: What happens if my company never registered for a Tax ID?

claims.text: Every taxable person shall register with the relevant tax authority and obtain a Tax ID for the purpose of compliance with tax obligations.

A taxable person who fails or refuses to register for tax under section 4 is liable to pay an administrative penalty of ₦50,000 in the first month in which the failure occurs and ₦25,000 for each subsequent month in which the failure continues.
A relevant tax authority may, based on the information available to it, register and issue a Tax ID to a person who should apply for one but failed to do so.
The relevant tax authority shall promptly notify a person registered and issued with a Tax ID in this way of the registration and Tax ID.
A statutory body or company that awards a contract to an unregistered person is liable to pay an administrative penalty of ₦5,000,000.
A Tax ID is a condition for entering into a contract with any federal or state ministry, department or agency and local government.
A person engaged in banking, insurance, stock-broking or other financial services in Nigeria shall ensure that every taxable person provides a Tax ID.

gaps: The total penalty over a given number of months would need a calculation, which is not done here.

Every taxable person shall register with the relevant tax authority and obtain a Tax ID for the purpose of compliance with tax obligations. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 4]

A taxable person who fails or refuses to register for tax under section 4 is liable to pay an administrative penalty of ₦50,000 in the first month in which the failure occurs and ₦25,000 for each subsequent month in which the failure continues. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 100]

A relevant tax authority may, based on the information available to it, register and issue a Tax ID to a person who should apply for one but failed to do so. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 7]

The relevant tax authority shall promptly notify a person registered and issued with a Tax ID in this way of the registration and Tax ID. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 7]

A statutory body or company that awards a contract to an unregistered person is liable to pay an administrative penalty of ₦5,000,000. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 100]

A Tax ID is a condition for entering into a contract with any federal or state ministry, department or agency and local government. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 8]

A person engaged in banking, insurance, stock-broking or other financial services in Nigeria shall ensure that every taxable person provides a Tax ID. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 8]

Tax is levied for each year of assessment on the total profits of every company, and for a small company the rate is 0%. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56]

A small company is a company that earns gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less per annum with total fixed assets not exceeding ₦250,000,000, and a business providing professional services shall not be classified as a small company. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company"]

Any other company is taxed at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56]

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56 (gazette page A 426)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company" (gazette page A 510)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": The gazette excludes any business providing professional services from being a small company; the National Assembly text has no such exclusion. (DR-151)

claims.text: Capital expenditure on furniture and fittings, including those used in buildings, for the purposes of trade or business is a type of qualifying capital expenditure (qualifying furniture and fittings expenditure).
Furniture and Fittings Expenditure is in Class 2 of Table I, which has a rate of 20%.

Where a person has incurred qualifying expenditure wholly and exclusively for the purposes of its trade or business, a capital allowance at the Table I rate is made for each year of assessment in the basis period for which the asset was used for the trade or business.
A capital allowance is made for a year of assessment if, at the end of a basis period, the person owns the asset and used it for the purposes of its trade or business.
Where the basis period for a year of assessment is less than one year, the allowance for that year is granted proportionately.

1% of qualifying capital expenditure is recorded in the capital allowance computation schedule for statistical purposes until the asset is disposed of. It is a notional amount and does not increase or reduce the capital allowance claimable.

The residue of a qualifying expenditure at any date is the total qualifying expenditure incurred on or before that date for the asset, less the total capital allowance made for that asset before that date.
An allowance is not made for a year of assessment unless it is claimed for that year, or the relevant tax authority is of the opinion that it would be just to the taxpayer and reasonable to do so.

An allowance is subtracted from the remainder of the assessable profits or income for the year. Where there is no remainder or an insufficient remainder, the deduction or the part not yet made is treated as a deduction for the next year and succeeding years until fully utilised.
Where the owner partly uses an asset for a trade or business, the allowance is apportioned to the trade or business as may be reasonable.

gaps: The yearly amount in naira needs a calculation of the rate on the cost or residue, which the passages do not do.
The passages do not say whether the furniture bought is qualifying furniture and fittings expenditure, or whether it is used for trade or business.
The passages do not say whether the allowance is worked on the original cost or on the reducing residue each year.

claims.text: A taxable person must, not later than the due date for rendering the relevant tax return prescribed by the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025, remit the excess to the Service where output VAT exceeds input VAT.
Where input VAT exceeds output VAT, a taxable person is entitled to use the excess as a credit against subsequent months.

Notes
- State and local government taxes and levies are outside the corpus this tool covers (v1). Answers come only from the provisions that are in the corpus.

The Nigeria Revenue Service (the Service) has exclusive responsibility to administer taxes on companies. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 3(1)]

The Service has exclusive responsibility to administer taxes as contained in the Act, including value added tax and exemptions from value added tax. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 3(1)]

The Service also has power to administer income tax, stamp duties and tax incentives. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 3(1)]

Every company must file a self-assessment return with the Service in the prescribed form at least once a year, whether or not it is liable to pay tax. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 11(1) to (2)]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The passages do not say what role, if any, a state revenue office has in collecting company income tax.
- The passages do not say whether a company's tax paid to a state office would count as payment.
- The passages do not state how a company that receives such a demand should respond.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 3(1) (gazette pages A 265, A 266)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 11(1) to (2) (gazette page A 269)

- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 3(1): In the cited text the Service has exclusive responsibility for the surcharge on fossil fuels; the National Assembly text omits it, and adds taxation of income from petroleum and value added tax to the taxes the Service has power to administer. My company sells furniture, has turnover of about ₦30 million a year and fixed assets worth ₦40 million. What company income tax rate applies to it?
</question>

cases.rendered:
Tax is levied for each year of assessment on the total profits of every company. A small company is taxed at 0%. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56]

Any other company is taxed at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56]

A small company is a company that earns gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less per annum with total fixed assets not exceeding ₦250,000,000. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company"]

Under that definition, any business providing professional services is not classified as a small company. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company"]

A separate effective tax rate rule applies to a company that is a constituent entity of an MNE group, or to any other company with an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- Whether the furniture business is a business providing professional services is not stated in the passages.
- Whether the company is a constituent entity of an MNE group is not stated in the passages.
- Whether the stated turnover and fixed assets are the company's gross turnover per annum and total fixed assets for the definition is not stated in the passages.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56 (gazette page A 426)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company" (gazette page A 510)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57 (gazette page A 426)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": The gazette excludes any business providing professional services from being a small company; the National Assembly text has no such exclusion. (DR-151)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)

cases.rationale: ntaa2025:s73(1)-(4): advance rulings on application by a taxable person, issued within 21 days or with written reasons.
cases.question: Can my company ask the tax service for a written ruling on how a law applies before we go ahead with a deal?

claims.text: An advance ruling may be issued for clarity, consistency and certainty on how any tax law is interpreted and applied, as long as it does not amend or replace the law.

The relevant tax authority may issue an advance ruling on an application by a taxable person within 21 days of receiving the application, or give reasons in writing for being unable to issue the ruling.
An application is to be made in the prescribed form and manner by a person who is a party to a tax related issue or transaction, or by two or more such parties.

The Act defines an advance ruling to include a written opinion or decision given to a taxpayer by the relevant tax authority on a transaction, proposed transaction or any tax matter, to give direction or clarification.

An application must contain the taxpayer's contact details, a complete description of the issue or transaction and its financial implications, if any, and a complete description of the impact on the tax liability of the taxpayer or any connected person.

An application must also contain details of any ongoing audit, previous correspondence and decisions on the issue, the statutory provisions or legal basis relied on, the reasons the ruling should be granted, and a written statement on whether the matter is before any tribunal or court of competent jurisdiction.
The tax authority may request additional information from an applicant, and where necessary shall give the applicant a reasonable opportunity to make representations or provide clarifications.
An applicant may withdraw an application at any time before a ruling is issued.

The tax authority may reject an application where it requires an opinion, conclusion or determination on the laws of a foreign country, an issue already before a court or tribunal of competent jurisdiction, the interpretation of the Constitution, or an issue that is academic, hypothetical, frivolous or vexatious.

The tax authority may also reject an application for a ruling that will interfere substantially with an ongoing audit, investigation or other proceeding involving the applicant or persons connected to the applicant.
A ruling's effect is limited to the applicant and the transaction for which it is given, and it is rendered on a set of facts before the tax authority and cannot be of general application.

An advance ruling is void where the issue or transaction described is materially different from what is actually carried out, where there is fraud, misrepresentation or non-disclosure of a material fact, or where an assumption or condition set by the tax authority is not satisfied or carried out by the taxpayer.

An advance ruling ceases to be effective where the tax law provision it concerned is repealed or amended in a way that materially affects it, or where a court overturns or modifies the interpretation it is based on.

The term company means a company as defined under the Companies and Allied Matters Act and a corporate body that may be formed under any other written law, and includes any association, whether incorporated in or outside Nigeria.

gaps: The passages do not say whether a company counts as a taxable person or taxpayer who may apply, or whether the tax service is the relevant tax authority.
The passages do not say what the prescribed form and manner of application are.
The passages do not say whether a particular deal is a tax related transaction.

claims.text: Where a Nigerian company declares dividend out of profits on which no tax is payable because there are no total profits, or because total profits are less than the dividend declared, the company paying the dividend is charged to tax at the rate prescribed in section 56 of the Act. This rule does not apply to dividends declared out of profits or gains that are exempt from income tax by the Act.
This rule does not apply to franked investment income as provided in the Act.

This rule does not apply to distributions by a real estate investment company to its shareholders from rental income and dividend income received on behalf of those shareholders, whether paid out of profits of the year of declaration or of previous reporting periods.

claims.text: A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria shall register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies.

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom a taxable supply is made in Nigeria and who is issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service.

VAT collected, withheld or self-accounted under section 155 shall be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction or as may be prescribed by the Service.

cases.rendered:
A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria shall register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

Where a non-resident person is making taxable supplies from outside Nigeria to persons in Nigeria, the taxable person to whom the supply is made in Nigeria shall withhold the VAT due on the supply and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

The Service may, by notice, appoint any person, including a non-resident supplier of taxable supplies, to collect the VAT and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

Where a person appointed by the Service has made a taxable supply to a taxable person in Nigeria, the taxable person does not have the obligation to withhold the VAT, except where the person appointed has failed to collect the VAT. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

A non-resident person that makes a taxable supply to a person in Nigeria may appoint a representative for the purpose of compliance with its VAT obligations. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom a taxable supply is made in Nigeria and who is issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

VAT collected, withheld or self-accounted under section 155 shall be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction or as may be prescribed by the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

The remission under section 155(1) and (2) shall be accompanied by a schedule showing the name, Tax ID and address of the contractor or supplier, invoice number, gross amount of invoice, amount of the VAT and the month to which the return relates. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The passages do not say whether the software services in the question are taxable supplies.
- The passages do not say whether the foreign online company has been appointed by the Service to collect VAT, or has failed to collect it.
- The passages do not say whether the person paying is a taxable person.
- The passages do not say whether the foreign company is a non-resident person for section 151; the definitions of foreign company do not address that.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151 (gazette pages A 472, A 473)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155 (gazette page A 474)

claims.text: Interest is a deductible expense where it is payable on debt employed in generating the income of the trade, business, profession or vocation, subject to the provisions of the Third Schedule.

Where a Nigerian company or a permanent establishment of a non-resident company in Nigeria incurs interest or similar expenditure on debt issued by a connected person, the excess interest is a disallowable deduction for the purposes of Chapter Two.

Excess interest means total interest paid or payable to a connected person that is above 30% of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation of the Nigerian company in that accounting period.
The limit does not apply to a Nigerian subsidiary of a foreign company that is engaged in the business of banking or insurance.

Interest expenditure not wholly deducted for an assessment year is carried forward to the following assessment year or years. It is allowed against the profits, if any, of any business carried on by the company and assessable for that year, to the extent permitted under paragraph (2) of the Schedule.
Interest expenditure is not carried forward for more than five assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the excess interest expenditure was first computed.

In the Third Schedule, debt means any loan, financial instrument, finance lease, financial derivative, or any arrangement that gives rise to interest, discounts or other finance charges that are deductible in computing income chargeable under the head profits and gains of business or profession.
A deduction is not allowed for any payment to a connected person that is not consistent with the Transfer Pricing Regulations issued by the Service.

<question>
My company borrowed money from a sister company. Is there a limit on the interest I can deduct?
</question>
<gaps>
<gap index="0">
The Transfer Pricing Regulations are not among the passages.

cases.rendered:
Interest is a deductible expense where it is payable on debt employed in generating the income of the trade, business, profession or vocation, subject to the provisions of the Third Schedule. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 20(1)(a) to (h)]

Where a Nigerian company or a permanent establishment of a non-resident company in Nigeria incurs interest or similar expenditure on debt issued by a connected person, the excess interest is a disallowable deduction for the purposes of Chapter Two. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Third Schedule]

Excess interest means total interest paid or payable to a connected person that is above 30% of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation of the Nigerian company in that accounting period. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Third Schedule]

The limit does not apply to a Nigerian subsidiary of a foreign company that is engaged in the business of banking or insurance. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Third Schedule]

Interest expenditure not wholly deducted for an assessment year is carried forward to the following assessment year or years. It is allowed against the profits, if any, of any business carried on by the company and assessable for that year, to the extent permitted under paragraph (2) of the Schedule. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Third Schedule]

Interest expenditure is not carried forward for more than five assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the excess interest expenditure was first computed. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Third Schedule]

In the Third Schedule, debt means any loan, financial instrument, finance lease, financial derivative, or any arrangement that gives rise to interest, discounts or other finance charges that are deductible in computing income chargeable under the head profits and gains of business or profession. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Third Schedule]

A deduction is not allowed for any payment to a connected person that is not consistent with the Transfer Pricing Regulations issued by the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 21(a) to (o)]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The passages do not say whether a sister company is a connected person, so they do not link the question to the limit.
- Working out the 30% limit and the amount of excess interest for the company's figures is a calculation not done here.
- The Transfer Pricing Regulations are not among the passages.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 20(1)(a) to (h) (gazette pages A 408, A 409)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Third Schedule (gazette page A 537)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 21(a) to (o) (gazette page A 410)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 20(1)(a) to (h): Cross-reference: the gazette cites Part IX of Chapter Two (Rates of Tax), the National Assembly text Part XI (Specialised Trade or Business), which is the intended reference; the gazette reading is a printing slip (DQ-14). Cited as printed. The other difference ('in the course of' / 'during') is wording. (DR-029)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Third Schedule: Only the gazette defines 'debt' for the deductible-interest rule (loan, financial instrument, finance lease, financial derivative or similar). (DR-176)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 21(a) to (o): Cross-reference: section 20(1)(h) (gazette) against section 20(j) (National Assembly). (DR-033)

<question>
Does a small company have to attach audited accounts to its annual tax return?
</question>
<gaps>

cases.rendered:
A company's self-assessment return must contain the audited financial statements, tax and capital allowances computation for the year of assessment in respect of the profit from each and every source computed. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 11(1) to (2)]

The return of a small company may contain a statement of accounts attested to by the taxpayer in place of audited financial statements. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 11(1) to (2)]

A small company is a company that earns gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less per annum with total fixed assets not exceeding ₦250,000,000. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company"]

A business providing professional services is not classified as a small company. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company"]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- Whether a particular company meets the small company definition on its turnover and fixed assets is a factual matter the passages do not decide.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 11(1) to (2) (gazette page A 269)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company" (gazette page A 510)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": The gazette excludes any business providing professional services from being a small company; the National Assembly text has no such exclusion. (DR-151)

claims.text: Where the relevant tax authority discovers or is of the opinion, at any time, that a taxable person liable to tax has not been assessed or has been assessed at less than what ought to have been charged, it may, within six years of the assessment, assess the person at the amount or additional amount that ought to have been charged.
The six-year limit does not stop the relevant tax authority from continuing a tax audit and raising an additional assessment where the tax audit started before the six-year limit expired.

Despite the time limit in subsection (1), where a taxable person makes a deliberate misstatement in connection with any tax imposed under the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025 or any other tax law, the relevant tax authority may at any time, and as often as necessary, assess the person for the amount needed to make good any loss of tax attributable to the deliberate misstatement.

All relevant facts are to be considered in working out the amount or additional amount of tax that should have been charged, even where those facts were not known when an earlier assessment or additional assessment was made for the same year.

The tax authority is not prevented from making an assessment or additional assessment for a year if it does not involve re-opening any issue on the same facts that was determined for that year under section 41(5) by agreement or on appeal.

gaps: The passages do not say whether the six years run from the original assessment date or from the filing date, so the exact start date for the question's year cannot be worked out.

A company involved in an arrangement with a related party shall also report the arrangement in the form and manner prescribed by the relevant tax authority. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

Where, in the opinion of a relevant tax authority, a company has entered into an arrangement with a related party which is not at arm's length, the authority may effect necessary adjustments to bring the arrangement in conformity to arm's length terms as provided under the Transfer Pricing Regulations. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

The relevant tax authority may make rules or regulations for the administration of section 192. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

For section 192, an "arrangement" includes any agreement, understanding, scheme, financial or commercial relation, transaction or series of transactions. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

For section 192, "arm's length terms and conditions" means such terms and conditions obtainable if the transaction or arrangement was between unrelated parties dealing in comparative circumstances. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

Section 192 makes the adjustment power subject to the Transfer Pricing Regulations. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

cases.question: My company made ₦120 million profit this year. How much company income tax will it pay?

claims.text: Tax is levied for each year of assessment on the total profits of every company. A small company is taxed at 0%.
Any other company is taxed at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act.

The total profits of a company are its total assessable profits from all sources, including chargeable gains, less any loss ascertained in accordance with subsection (6) and capital allowance in accordance with Part I of the First Schedule.

Capital allowance is the amount relating to qualifying capital expenditure incurred in generating the assessable profits. It is prorated where an asset is only partly used to generate assessable profits, but it is not prorated where non-taxable income is less than 10% of the company's total income.

A company must include dividend income in its profits, gross of any tax paid or deducted at source. Dividends a Nigerian company receives by way of shares of the paying company are not included in its profits chargeable to tax.

Where the effective tax rate of a company in a year of assessment is less than 15%, the company shall recompute and pay an additional tax that makes its effective tax rate equal to 15%. This applies to a constituent entity of an MNE group and to any other company with an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment.

<question>
My company made ₦120 million profit this year. How much company income tax will it pay?
</question>
<gaps>
<gap index="0">
The company's turnover, whether it is part of an MNE group, and its covered tax paid are not known, so whether the 15% effective tax rate rule applies is not known.
</gap>
</gaps>

cases.rendered:
Tax is levied for each year of assessment on the total profits of every company. A small company is taxed at 0%. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56]

Any other company is taxed at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56]

The total profits of a company are its total assessable profits from all sources, including chargeable gains, less any loss ascertained in accordance with subsection (6) and capital allowance in accordance with Part I of the First Schedule. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4)]

Capital allowance is the amount relating to qualifying capital expenditure incurred in generating the assessable profits. It is prorated where an asset is only partly used to generate assessable profits, but it is not prorated where non-taxable income is less than 10% of the company's total income. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4)]

A company must include dividend income in its profits, gross of any tax paid or deducted at source. Dividends a Nigerian company receives by way of shares of the paying company are not included in its profits chargeable to tax. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8]

Where the effective tax rate of a company in a year of assessment is less than 15%, the company shall recompute and pay an additional tax that makes its effective tax rate equal to 15%. This applies to a constituent entity of an MNE group and to any other company with an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The meaning of a small company is not in the passages, so whether the company is small is not known.
- The company's total profits after losses and capital allowances are not known, so the tax cannot be worked out from the profit figure alone.
- The calculation of the tax amount at the applicable rate is not done here.
- Section 56 does not state the turnover or other limits for a small company, and no definition is among the passages.
- The company's turnover, whether it is part of an MNE group, and its covered tax paid are not known, so whether the 15% effective tax rate rule applies is not known.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56 (gazette page A 426)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4) (gazette pages A 412, A 413)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8 (gazette page A 397)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57 (gazette page A 426)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4): The National Assembly text requires companies in the priority sector to obtain a certificate of acceptance from the Industrial Inspectorate Department for qualifying capital expenditure; the gazette has no such condition. (DR-039)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8: Cross-reference: the gazette cites section 51 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, the National Assembly text section 50. (DR-007, DR-008)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)

cases.question: Under section 191 of the Nigeria Tax Act, where do objections and appeals go?

claims.text: Section 191 says the provisions on objections and appeals under Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025 apply to a direction made under that section.

Section 191 lets a relevant tax authority disregard a disposition or an artificial or fictitious transaction, or direct adjustments to liability to tax, and issue an assessment or additional assessment.

gaps: Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, which section 191 refers to, is not among the passages, so the objection and appeal route under it is not shown.
The passages on objections (section 41) sit in Chapter Two of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, not Chapter Four, so they cannot be treated as the Chapter Four provisions that section 191 names.
